name: Angelman Syndrome

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Williams et al. Consensus Criteria for Angelman Syndrome (2006 Update)

criteria.description: Severe developmental delay / intellectual disability with minimal or no speech
Movement or balance disorder (ataxia, tremulous movement of limbs)
Behavioral uniqueness: frequent laughter/smiling, apparent happy demeanor, excitability with hand-flapping
Speech impairment with minimal or no use of words; receptive language better than expressive
Microcephaly (deceleration of head growth by age 2)
Loss of maternal UBE3A expression confirmed by genetic testing

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Clinical features (all 4 major clinical criteria) confirmed by genetic testing showing loss of maternal UBE3A expression. Genetic test is confirmatory but clinical diagnosis is primary.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Four genetic mechanisms: maternal deletion of 15q11-q13 (~70%), paternal UPD (~3-5%), imprinting defect (~3-5%), UBE3A mutation (~10-15%). ~10% have no identifiable molecular mechanism. Deletion class tends to have more severe phenotype.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Frequent unprovoked laughter and happy demeanor
pathognomonic.notes: Easily provoked and sustained laughter; apparent happy affect is highly characteristic

pathognomonic.symptomName: Severe intellectual disability with absent or minimal speech
pathognomonic.notes: Most individuals use fewer than 5-6 words; nonverbal communication relatively preserved

common.notes: Multiple seizure types; often difficult to control; onset typically <3 years

occasional.notes: Lighter hair, skin, and eyes than family members; due to OCA2 gene in deleted region

laboratory: Routine laboratory studies are typically normal
EEG showing characteristic pattern: high-amplitude 2-3 Hz slow waves, often most prominent posteriorly
Rhythmic theta activity (4-6 Hz) over frontal regions
imaging: Brain MRI typically normal or nonspecific (mild cortical atrophy or cerebellar changes in some)
MRI may show myelination delay in infancy
genetic: DNA methylation analysis at 15q11-q13 (first-line test; detects deletions, UPD, and some imprinting defects)
Maternal deletion of 15q11-q13 (~70%, detected by FISH/microarray)
UBE3A gene mutation (~10-15%, requires gene sequencing)
~10% clinically diagnosed but no molecular abnormality found

distinguishingFeatures: Hyperphagia and obesity are hallmarks of PWS
Hypotonia in infancy but no seizures typically
Different behavioral phenotype (stubbornness rather than happy demeanor)
Rett shows regression after period of normal development
Distinctive facial features (deep-set eyes, wide mouth)
Overlap in happy affect and absent speech
Also has happy demeanor but different pattern

redFlags: Refractory seizures requiring aggressive anticonvulsant management
Severe sleep disturbance impacting quality of life
Recurrence risk counseling critical (depends on genetic mechanism)
references: Williams CA, et al. Angelman syndrome 2005: updated consensus for diagnostic criteria. Am J Med Genet A. 2006;140(5):413-418.
Buiting K, et al. Angelman syndrome - insights into a rare neurogenetic disorder. Nat Rev Neurol. 2016;12(10):584-593.
Dagli AI, et al. Angelman Syndrome. GeneReviews. Updated 2021.
Margolis SS, et al. Angelman syndrome. Neurotherapeutics. 2015;12(3):641-650.
